name: Interglossa
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.verdict: a reachable source states the stress pattern
earlier_scan.note: Fixed penultimate stress (per Hogben's design; hiatus kept in vowel-final sequences, e.g. nesia stressed on e).

new_statements.quote: Non-Aryan-speaking people who find difficulty with compound consonants and closed syllables (as in blinding or trumpet) will find that some pigeon-holes of the semantic schema offer alternatives of the Yo-ko-ha-ma or To-ky-o type (cf. itinero travel, nesia island). All polysyllables end with a vowel. Unless the last two syllables are both vowels (-io, -ia, etc.), the stress is on the penultimate one, e.g. billEta, permIto. If the word ends with two vowels, the stress is on the antepenultimate syllable, e.g. nEsia and orientAtio.
new_statements.citation: Hogben, Lancelot. 1943. Interglossa: A draft of an auxiliary for a democratic world order, being an attempt to apply semantic principles to language design. Harmondsworth: Penguin Books (Pelican). Chapter II 'The Essential Grammar of Interglossa', section (a) Phonetics.
new_statements.locator: Part I, Ch. II 'The Essential Grammar of Interglossa', sect. (a) 'Phonetics', final paragraph of the section (Ch. II begins on p. 30 per the book's Contents, so the sentence falls on p. 30 or 31; the transcription carries no page breaks). In the saved extraction: line 712.

The quoted passage is there word for word: '.. All polysyllables end with a vowel. Unless the last two syllables are both vowels ( -io, -ia, etc.), the stress is on the penultimate one, e.g. billEta, permIto. If the word ends with two vowels, the stress is on the antepenultimate syllable, e.g. nEsia and orientAtio.' Only differences from the report's quote are stray spaces left wher…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Designed fixed stress: every polysyllable ends in a vowel and is stressed on the penultimate syllable (billéta, permíto); when the word ends in a two-vowel sequence (-ia, -io, etc., kept as hiatus, each vowel its own syllable) stress falls on the antepenult, i.e. on the syllable before the vowel sequence (nésia, orientátio). Equivalently: stress the last vowel that precedes the final vowel(s) but is separated from the word end by at least one consonant-onset syllable -- a Latin-like penult rule with the -ia/-io class treated as antepenultimate.
new_statements.exceptions: Only the stated sub-rule: words ending in two vowels (-io, -ia, etc.) take antepenultimate stress (nEsia, orientAtio). Monosyllabic particles (and the clipped forms uN, aD, noN, nuN, eX) fall outside the rule since it is stated for polysyllables. Hogben flags the whole phonetics section as 'preliminary, and at this stage very tentative'.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rule for citation forms of vocables, prescribed by the language's designer (normative design statement, not a description of usage). No phrase-level prosody discussed apart from a remark elsewhere (item on cleisto, Ch. VI) about English contrastive sentence stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Source is the designer's own 1943 draft of Interglossa (inte1261, ISO igs). Not to be conflated with its descendant Glosa (Ashby & Clark, 1970s-; Glottolog glos1234), whose spelling and some conventions differ; the Glosa history PDF saved here says nothing about Interglossa stress.

sources.note: Ch. II sect. (a) Phonetics: all polysyllables end in a vowel; stress on the penultimate syllable (billEta, permIto) unless the word ends in two vowels (-io, -ia etc.), in which case stress is antepenultimate (nEsia, orientAtio).

Paraphrases Hogben: 'The stress is generally on the penultimate syllable, e.g. billeta, nesia.. Hogben rather keeps a hiatus, stating that the stress in nesia is on the antepenultimate syllable.' Secondary; points to the Google Sites transcription.
